newsitem.title: JAPAN: Lloyd's of London sees 1996 profit 600-700 mln stg.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's of London sees 1996 profit 600-700 mln stg.

text.p: Profits for the insurance market Lloyd's of London in 1996 are likely to be around 600 to 700 million pounds after estimated profits of around one billion pounds for 1995, chairman David Rowland said on Tuesday.
Lloyd's reports results three years in arrears. In April, it said underwriting profits before tax and after members' personal expenses for 1994 totalled 1.005 billion pounds.
Rowland told a British Chamber of Commerce luncheon in Tokyo that its profits forecast for 1995 would be the similar to 1994.
But he said that he expected profits would fall in 1996.
"1996 (profits) will be down a bit because the rates came off in the international market, but still likely to be in the order of six or seven hundred million pounds," Rowland said.
His forecasts are within market expectations.
Lloyd's returned to profit in 1993 after five years of record losses totalling more than eight billion pounds which had threatened the very survival of the world's oldest insurance market.

Rowland also said while there was tension between corporate funds and Names, its traditional individual backers which the funds have been increasingly replacing, the introduction of corporate members in 1994 had produced "a situation of fairness in the market".
He said there were reasons why the capital structure must change for the future, but did not elaborate.

"I believe it's a situation that we can continue to manage and the old members will see certainly that they have excellent profits since 1993...and we shall deal with them fairly in the future," he said.
Rowland added that it did not really matter which government body oversaw Lloyd's after the Labour government's sweeping reforms of Britain's financial regulatory system.
Industry observers say the Treasury may well take over the regulation of insurance from the Department of Trade and Industry after the shake-up, though no decision has been made.
Earlier this month, the insurance market announced it favoured giving up 300 years of self-regulation for supervision by an external authority, specifically the Securities and Investments Board.
"I don't care. I only want the best, the most efficient form of regulation. I don't care where it is," Rowland said.
